Volatility Dents Consumer Mood of Wealthier Americans
 
Plus, struggles with Roth conversions and a look at small-cap and value stocks
 
 
BING GUAN/REUTERS
 

Consumer sentiment improved in November, according to the University of Michigan’s monthly survey, yet it remains near historically low levels that reflect Americans’ widespread economic frustrations.

 

Stock-market volatility dented the mood among wealthier Americans who own more assets, said Joanne Hsu, the survey’s director. By contrast, sentiment improved among low- and middle-wealth consumers.

 

Below, some of the best analysis and insight from WSJ writers and columnists, the Dow Jones Newswires team and occasionally beyond, on investing, the wealth-management business and more.

Market Talk

 

From Dow Jones Newswires

 

Treasury yields are likely to trend lower as market volatility spurs demand for bonds, SanJac Alpha’s Andrew Wells says. He is buying seven- to 10-year Treasurys as markets rotate out of risk assets. “We turned, I’d say in September, maybe early September, we began to turn more bullish on rates,” Wells says. “So we began to turn constructive on the longer end of the curve…and have been doing that since.” Wells expects Treasury buying to pick up further amid potential 1Q volatility around government debt ceiling debates. “We think there’s definitely some room to go.” (Paulo Trevisani, paulo.trevisani@wsj.com)

 

Canadian energy stocks will continue to benefit from a slow off-ramp from the U.S.-Iran conflict, RBC analysts say in a report. While the sector has been “whipsawed by headlines” around Middle East tensions this year, RBC expects oil prices to stay elevated, forecasting crude to average $88 a barrel over the next four quarters. “There is no easy off ramp to the conflict,” the analysts noted, adding that they view “the recent repricing of geopolitical risks post midterms as premature.” RBC remains overweight energy, noting the sector “continues to have the most positives” in its estimates, led by lower debt, high free-cash-flow yields and a supportive domestic policy backdrop. (Adriano Marchese, adriano.marchese@wsj.com)
